Minkowski's Inequality

The LpL^pLp triangle inequality — ∥f+g∥p≤∥f∥p+∥g∥p\|f+g\|_p \le \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p∥f+g∥p​≤∥f∥p​+∥g∥p​ on [0,1][0,1][0,1]. With f(t)=taf(t) = t^af(t)=ta, g(t)=(1−t)bg(t) = (1-t)^bg(t)=(1−t)b, sliding ppp opens and closes the gap between the two bars. At p=1p = 1p=1 linearity of the integral closes the gap to 0.

∥f+g∥p≤∥f∥p+∥g∥p(1≤p<∞)\|f+g\|_p \le \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p \quad (1 \le p < \infty)∥f+g∥p​≤∥f∥p​+∥g∥p​(1≤p<∞)
∥f∥p=(∫01∣f∣p)1/p\|f\|_p = \left(\int_0^1 |f|^p\right)^{1/p}∥f∥p​=(∫01​∣f∣p)1/p

Prove completely, starting from homogeneity ∥cf∥p=c∥f∥p\|cf\|_p = c\|f\|_p∥cf∥p​=c∥f∥p​, that Minkowski's inequality is an equality when g=c fg = c\,fg=cf for a constant c≥0c \ge 0c≥0. g=cf (c≥0)  ⇒  ∥f+g∥p=(1+c)∥f∥p=∥f∥p+∥g∥pg = cf\ (c \ge 0) \;\Rightarrow\; \|f+g\|_p = (1+c)\|f\|_p = \|f\|_p + \|g\|_pg=cf (c≥0)⇒∥f+g∥p​=(1+c)∥f∥p​=∥f∥p​+∥g∥p​
a=b=0:∥f∥p=∥g∥p=1,∥f+g∥p=2a = b = 0:\quad \|f\|_p = \|g\|_p = 1,\quad \|f+g\|_p = 2a=b=0:∥f∥p​=∥g∥p​=1,∥f+g∥p​=2
Show proof
  1. First prove homogeneity. For c≥0c \ge 0c≥0, ∥cf∥pp=∫01∣cf∣p=∫01cp∣f∣p=cp∥f∥pp\|cf\|_p^p = \int_0^1 |cf|^p = \int_0^1 c^p |f|^p = c^p \|f\|_p^p∥cf∥pp​=∫01​∣cf∣p=∫01​cp∣f∣p=cp∥f∥pp​, so taking ppp-th roots gives ∥cf∥p=c∥f∥p\|cf\|_p = c\|f\|_p∥cf∥p​=c∥f∥p​.
  2. If g=cfg = cfg=cf with c≥0c \ge 0c≥0, then f+g=(1+c)ff + g = (1+c)ff+g=(1+c)f, so by homogeneity ∥f+g∥p=∥(1+c)f∥p=(1+c)∥f∥p=∥f∥p+c∥f∥p=∥f∥p+∥cf∥p=∥f∥p+∥g∥p\|f+g\|_p = \|(1+c)f\|_p = (1+c)\|f\|_p = \|f\|_p + c\|f\|_p = \|f\|_p + \|cf\|_p = \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p∥f+g∥p​=∥(1+c)f∥p​=(1+c)∥f∥p​=∥f∥p​+c∥f∥p​=∥f∥p​+∥cf∥p​=∥f∥p​+∥g∥p​ — equality holds.
  3. For the scene: a=b=0a = b = 0a=b=0 gives f(t)=t0≡1f(t) = t^0 \equiv 1f(t)=t0≡1 and g(t)=(1−t)0≡1g(t) = (1-t)^0 \equiv 1g(t)=(1−t)0≡1, so g=1⋅fg = 1 \cdot fg=1⋅f. Hence ∥f∥2=(∫011 dt)1/2=1\|f\|_2 = \left(\int_0^1 1\,dt\right)^{1/2} = 1∥f∥2​=(∫01​1dt)1/2=1, ∥g∥2=1\|g\|_2 = 1∥g∥2​=1, ∥f+g∥2=∥2∥2=2\|f+g\|_2 = \|2\|_2 = 2∥f+g∥2​=∥2∥2​=2, matching the right side ∥f∥2+∥g∥2=2\|f\|_2 + \|g\|_2 = 2∥f∥2​+∥g∥2​=2 — the gap is exactly 0. (Note: at p=1p = 1p=1 equality always holds by linearity ∫(f+g)=∫f+∫g\int (f+g) = \int f + \int g∫(f+g)=∫f+∫g. The deeper equality condition — that the Hölder steps need ∣f∣p|f|^p∣f∣p proportional to ∣g∣q|g|^q∣g∣q — includes this proportional case.)

Show that Minkowski's inequality fails for 0<p<10 < p < 10<p<1. First prove that for f,g≥0f, g \ge 0f,g≥0 the inequality reverses to ∥f+g∥p≥∥f∥p+∥g∥p\|f+g\|_p \ge \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p∥f+g∥p​≥∥f∥p​+∥g∥p​, then compute the concrete counterexample p=12p = \frac12p=21​, f(t)=tf(t) = tf(t)=t, g(t)=1−tg(t) = 1-tg(t)=1−t directly and verify numerically that ∥f+g∥1/2=1>89=∥f∥1/2+∥g∥1/2\|f+g\|_{1/2} = 1 > \frac89 = \|f\|_{1/2} + \|g\|_{1/2}∥f+g∥1/2​=1>98​=∥f∥1/2​+∥g∥1/2​.

0<p<1:(f+g)p≥fp+gp  ⇒  ∥f+g∥p≥∥f∥p+∥g∥p0 < p < 1:\quad (f+g)^p \ge f^p + g^p \;\Rightarrow\; \|f+g\|_p \ge \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p0<p<1:(f+g)p≥fp+gp⇒∥f+g∥p​≥∥f∥p​+∥g∥p​
p=12:∥f∥1/2=∥g∥1/2=49,∥f+g∥1/2=1>89p = \tfrac12:\quad \|f\|_{1/2} = \|g\|_{1/2} = \tfrac49,\quad \|f+g\|_{1/2} = 1 > \tfrac89p=21​:∥f∥1/2​=∥g∥1/2​=94​,∥f+g∥1/2​=1>98​
Show proof
  1. Let 0<p<10 < p < 10<p<1 and f,g≥0f, g \ge 0f,g≥0. Pointwise (f+g)p≥fp+gp(f+g)^p \ge f^p + g^p(f+g)p≥fp+gp (the base f+g≥max⁡(f,g)f+g \ge \max(f, g)f+g≥max(f,g) with positive exponent), so integrating gives ∥f+g∥pp≥∥f∥pp+∥g∥pp\|f+g\|_p^p \ge \|f\|_p^p + \|g\|_p^p∥f+g∥pp​≥∥f∥pp​+∥g∥pp​. With r=1p>1r = \frac1p > 1r=p1​>1 we have (A+B)r≥Ar+Br(A+B)^r \ge A^r + B^r(A+B)r≥Ar+Br for A,B≥0A, B \ge 0A,B≥0 (e.g. (1+t)r≥1+tr(1+t)^r \ge 1 + t^r(1+t)r≥1+tr for t≥0t \ge 0t≥0), hence ∥f+g∥p≥(∥f∥pp+∥g∥pp)1/p≥∥f∥p+∥g∥p\|f+g\|_p \ge \big(\|f\|_p^p + \|g\|_p^p\big)^{1/p} \ge \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p∥f+g∥p​≥(∥f∥pp​+∥g∥pp​)1/p≥∥f∥p​+∥g∥p​ — the inequality reverses.
  2. Concretely, take p=12p = \frac12p=21​, f(t)=tf(t) = tf(t)=t, g(t)=1−tg(t) = 1-tg(t)=1−t. Since ∫01t dt=23\int_0^1 \sqrt{t}\,dt = \frac23∫01​t​dt=32​, we get ∥f∥1/2=(23)2=49≈0.444444\|f\|_{1/2} = \left(\frac23\right)^2 = \frac49 \approx 0.444444∥f∥1/2​=(32​)2=94​≈0.444444, and by symmetry ∥g∥1/2=49\|g\|_{1/2} = \frac49∥g∥1/2​=94​. So the right side is 49+49=89≈0.888889\frac49 + \frac49 = \frac89 \approx 0.88888994​+94​=98​≈0.888889. But f+g≡1f + g \equiv 1f+g≡1, so ∥f+g∥1/2=(∫011 dt)2=1\|f+g\|_{1/2} = \left(\int_0^1 1\,dt\right)^2 = 1∥f+g∥1/2​=(∫01​1dt)2=1. Hence 1>891 > \frac891>98​ — Minkowski's inequality breaks, and the gap is −19≈−0.111111-\frac19 \approx -0.111111−91​≈−0.111111, negative (also confirmed by numerical integration).
  3. The exact failure point of the standard proof is also clear: Hölder's inequality needs the conjugate exponent q=pp−1>1q = \frac{p}{p-1} > 1q=p−1p​>1, but for p<1p < 1p<1 we get q<0q < 0q<0, so the Hölder step itself is unavailable. That is why Minkowski's inequality essentially requires p≥1p \ge 1p≥1.
